"Range" refers to the space between two limits — a low point and a high point. Everything within those two limits belongs to that range.

Think of a thermometer. If the temperature in your city this week went from 18°C to 34°C, then the range of temperatures was 18°C to 34°C. That gap — from the lowest to the highest — is the range.

This core idea of "a span between limits" gives birth to most of the word's meanings. Keep this idea in mind as you read further.

1. A span of values, amounts, or levels

This is the most common and fundamental meaning. A range here is the entire stretch between a minimum and a maximum.

  • "The shoes are available in a price range of ₹500 to ₹5,000." (The cheapest is ₹500; the most expensive is ₹5,000. Everything in between is the range.)
  • "The job is open to candidates in the age range of 21 to 35."
  • "Normal human body temperature falls in the range of 36.1°C to 37.2°C."

Notice that a range always implies two boundaries — a floor and a ceiling — and the range is everything in between.

2. Variety or scope (a collection of different things)

When someone says "a range of things," they mean a collection or variety — multiple different things belonging to the same category.

  • "The restaurant offers a range of vegetarian dishes." (Several different vegetarian dishes.)
  • "She has experience in a wide range of fields, including medicine, law, and engineering."
  • "The store sells a range of laptops to suit every budget."

Here, "range" is less about numbers and more about breadth. A wide range = many different kinds. A narrow range = only a few kinds.

3. The maximum distance something can reach or travel

This meaning is about how far something can go or work before it runs out of power, fuel, or effectiveness.

  • "The electric car has a range of 500 kilometres on a single charge." (It can travel up to 500 km before needing to recharge.)
  • "The missile has a range of 300 kilometres." (It can hit targets up to 300 km away.)
  • "This Wi-Fi router has a range of 30 metres." (The signal works up to 30 metres away.)

Think of it as: how far can this thing reach before it stops working?

4. The distance between you and a target (especially in shooting or military contexts)

Here, "range" means the distance between a person and the thing they are looking at, shooting at, or targeting.

  • "The soldier fired at the enemy from a range of 200 metres." (The enemy was 200 metres away.)
  • "The sniper hit the target at close range." (Very short distance.)
  • "At this range, even a beginner can hit the bullseye." (At this distance.)

Related phrases:

  • At close range = from very nearby.
  • At long range = from far away.
  • Out of range = too far away to reach or hit.
  • Within range = close enough to reach or hit.

5. A place for practicing shooting

A shooting range (often just called "the range") is a controlled area, either indoors or outdoors, where people go to practice firing guns or bows.

  • "He went to the range on Sunday to practice his aim."
  • "The army has a firing range outside the city."

6. A row or chain of mountains

A mountain range is a long, connected line of mountains that form a natural group or series.

  • "The Himalayas are the world's highest mountain range."
  • "The Rocky Mountain range runs through western North America."
  • "We could see the entire range of peaks from the hilltop."

The word "range" fits well here because the mountains extend in a line — they span from one point to another, much like a range of values does.

7. Open land for grazing (especially in North America)

In farming and ranching, a range is a large, open stretch of land where cattle, sheep, or horses roam and feed freely — without fences or enclosures.

  • "The cowboys drove the cattle across the open range."
  • "The horses were let loose on the range to graze."
  • "Life on the range was tough and lonely for early settlers."

This is especially common in the context of the American West. You may have heard the classic song "Home on the Range," which is about living freely on this open land.

8. A cooking appliance (a stove)

In many English-speaking countries, especially the United States, a kitchen range is a cooking appliance that combines a stovetop (burners on top) and an oven (for baking, below or alongside).

  • "She bought a new gas range for her kitchen."
  • "The range has four burners and a large oven."

This is basically what many people call a "stove" or "cooker." The word "range" for this comes from old kitchen appliances that had a wide surface to cook on — literally a range of cooking surfaces.

9. The span of notes a voice or instrument can produce (music)

In music, range means the full spread of notes — from the lowest note to the highest note — that a voice or instrument is capable of producing.

  • "She has an impressive vocal range — she can sing very deep notes and very high notes."
  • "The piano has a wider range than a guitar."
  • "His voice has a range of three octaves."

A wide range = can hit both very low and very high notes. A narrow range = can only sing or play notes that are close together in pitch.

10. In mathematics and statistics

In statistics, the range is a precise calculation: it is the difference between the highest value and the lowest value in a set of data.

For example, if a student's test scores over 5 tests were: 55, 60, 70, 80, 95 — the range is 95 − 55 = 40.

  • "The range of scores in the exam was 40 points." (The gap between the best and worst score.)
  • "A large range tells us that the data is spread out."

In mathematics (specifically functions), "range" has a related but more technical meaning: it is the set of all possible output values of a function. (For learners just getting started, this is a more advanced concept, but the underlying idea — what values are possible — connects back to the core meaning of range as a span or set of possible values.)

It helps to see that almost all these meanings share the same spirit:

  • A span between limits → price range, age range, temperature range, vocal range, statistical range.
  • How far something can reach → missile range, car range, Wi-Fi range, shooting range (distance to target).
  • A stretch of land or mountains → mountain range, open range (these literally "extend" or "stretch" in space).
  • A place to practise within limits → shooting range.
  • A wide variety → "a range of products" (many options spanning a category).
  • A kitchen appliance → this is the most unrelated in feel, though historically it came from the idea of a wide surface spanning across a fireplace.

• A wide range of → many varieties of (e.g., "a wide range of options")
  • A narrow range of → few varieties of; limited options
  • Within range → close enough to reach or be reached
  • Out of range → too far to reach or be reached
  • At close range → from very nearby
  • At long range → from far away
  • In the range of → approximately; somewhere between (e.g., "the cost will be in the range of ₹10,000 to ₹15,000")
  • Full range → the entire extent, every possibility (e.g., "she showed the full range of her emotions")
  • Mountain range → a connected chain of mountains
  • Shooting range / firing range → a place to practise shooting
  • Home on the range → an expression meaning life on the open, free land (used poetically or nostalgically)

To sum it up in plain words:

"Range" as a noun most often means the full stretch between two limits — be it a span of numbers, a stretch of land, the distance something can travel, the variety in a collection, the notes a voice can hit, or the distance between you and a target. In a kitchen, it's a stove. At a gun club, it's where you practise. But in almost every use, the word carries the feeling of extent — of something that stretches from one point to another.
